column4: The section reads the odd oath as kin seeking what is owed for a slain relative; this law prescribes qisas for the killed while allowing a brother to accept compensation and requiring fair payment. It gives that family claim a bounded legal course.
“Life in qisas” states why the retaliation law protects the living, and its address to “people of understanding” echoes the surah’s oath being directed to ذِي حِجْرٍ.

The section’s dictionary note connects the valley word at 89:9 to diyah; this rule explicitly requires دِيَةٌ مُّسَلَّمَةٌ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ, compensation delivered to the slain believer’s family after accidental killing.

This is the section’s precise guardian-and-limit counterpart: the wrongfully slain person’s ولي is given authority, but is forbidden to exceed the bounds in killing. It distinguishes justice for a victim from a new blood excess.
The law “a life for a life” and “wounds are subject to qisas” makes measured retaliation explicit, while the same verse also names pardon as an alternative.

The source section’s dictionary branch on م ث ل describes a punishment made an example; this verse says earlier مُثُلَات had already passed before those demanding evil quickly, supplying the direct Qur’anic formulation.
The word مِرْصَادًا repeats the section’s 89:14 word: here Hell is lying in wait, making the watch-and-recompense image concrete.

The section explicitly glosses its source form وَتَرَهُ حَقَّهُ as reducing someone’s right, and cites يَتِرَكُمْ here: in its battle exhortation God promises not to diminish the believers’ deeds, the divine opposite of an unpaid or reduced due.
The just scales do not wrong a soul even by a mustard-seed weight; this gives exact measure to the section’s claim that recompense is kept rather than lost.
The opened record leaves out neither small nor great deeds; it makes the section’s “the return does not disappear” claim visible as an account with no omissions.
The tiniest good is seen, a direct counterpart to the section’s assurance that a person’s deed will not be diminished or lost.
The following verse gives the matching result for the tiniest evil, completing the account on the adverse side of the section’s reckoning.
Every soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged; this is the precise reckoning behind the section’s image of a return held ready.
This verse likewise says each soul is recompensed for its earning without injustice, spelling out the moral account implied by the Lord’s mirsad.
“What is with you passes, but what is with God remains” directly develops the section’s claim that the return is not lost but stays in place; the verse then promises recompense to the patient.

The verse distinguishes deliberate killing of a believer from 4:92’s accidental-killing compensation and names a severe divine recompense. It extends the section’s movement from a human family claim to a penalty no guardian can settle.
The next ayah identifies the ones for whom the 78:21 mirsad waits: the transgressors. That supplies the target of the waiting image in the cited verse.
The same passage calls the punishment جَزَاءً وِفَاقًا, a fitting recompense; this is a direct formulation of the measured return kept ready in the section.

The section links قَسَمٌ to oaths distributed among a slain person’s guardians; here, after a death during travel, two witnesses swear by God about a bequest when doubt arises. The legal setting is a testament rather than homicide, but it is a specific death-linked oath procedure.

Within the sacred-month rule, the verse says a violation may be answered in equal measure. Its setting is armed conflict rather than a murdered person’s guardian, but it states the same bounded-return principle.
If retaliation is taken, this verse limits it to the harm received, then says patience is better; it gives the section’s blood-return image an explicit boundary and alternative.
The verse allows one harmed to answer in like measure and promises divine help if that person is wronged again, a specific parallel for measured response and the Lord’s role beyond human claimants.
“The recompense of an injury is an injury like it,” followed by pardon and reconciliation, directly joins equivalent return to the alternative of mercy that bounds the section’s vendetta image.
Evil is repaid only with its like, while good receives better; this is a concise statement of the proportional account the section hears in mirsad.
The verse says an evil deed is repaid only with its like, while good is multiplied; it distinguishes exact liability from generosity in the divine account.
The section singles out Thamud cutting rock in the valley; here the people of al-Hijr carve houses into mountains while feeling secure, a close recurrence of their rock-cut dwelling scene.
The next ayah says a cry seized the mountain-house builders in the morning, giving one of the section’s named exemplary peoples a concrete punishment.

This prescription to the Children of Israel says that killing a soul without a life-for-life cause is like killing all humanity, while saving one is like saving all. It deepens the section’s claim that qisas has life as its purpose.

The next step in the death-and-bequest procedure replaces witnesses found to have sinned with others who swear by God. This is a distinct legal setting from the section’s qasama, but it shows an oath being used to correct a disputed claim after a death.
Each soul is held to what it earned; this contrasts the family’s human effort to claim blood with personal divine liability that cannot be shifted to another.
The warning says one soul cannot avail another and no ransom will be accepted, a boundary on what any human kin or guardian can accomplish at the final reckoning.
This verse introduces the two sons of Adam whose conflict continues in 5:28–30; that neighboring account supplies the family setting for the refusal and killing named in those following ayat.
The threatened brother warns that killing him would bring the other into the company of the Fire; the account locates consequence in divine judgment rather than a human guardian’s retaliation.

The story then states that one brother kills the other. This is a direct kin-murder scene beside the section’s imagined murdered relative, though the story proceeds to guilt and burial rather than a blood claim.

The section’s secondary dictionary form for وَتَرَ is “to reduce his right”; Shuʿayb similarly forbids بِخْس, reducing people’s due in measure. The domain is trade rather than blood compensation, but the concrete wrong is the same deprivation of what is owed.
This command not to reduce people’s things repeats the section’s dictionary sense of a right made short, here in a warning against commercial fraud and corruption.

The opening woe names the mutaffifin, the underweighers; the next two ayat specify their practice of taking full measure and giving less, a concrete instance of the right-reduction named in the section.
These traders take their measure in full for themselves, establishing the one-sided exchange that the section’s language of diminished rights makes perceptible.
When they measure or weigh for others, they give less; this is a precise transactional picture of withholding what is due.
The passage asks whether these underweighers expect to be raised, explicitly joining the reduced measure in 83:1–3 to future reckoning.
The next ayah identifies the accounting horizon as a great day, completing the fraud-to-recompense link.
People stand before the Lord of the worlds on that day; this gives the underweighers’ present short measure the future accounting that the section names as the Lord’s mirsad.

The same مرصد root can describe people sitting in ambush at every lookout in a wartime command. That is human tactical waiting, a different and hostile use from the section’s divine watch over an account.

The mosque built as إِرْصَادًا is a human ambush serving opposition to God and His Messenger; this other use of the section’s ر ص د root makes the moral difference from the Lord’s just waiting matter.

This verse uses رَصَدًا for watchers placed before and behind a chosen messenger. It develops the watchfulness sense of the section’s mirsad, though here the watchers guard a message rather than await recompense.
The neighboring verse says God encompasses what they have and counts everything; it adds exact enumeration to the messenger-guarding scene and to the section’s claim that nothing due is lost.
An observer ready is assigned to each spoken word; it parallels the section’s watchman image by making human acts continuously observed before their accounting.
The passage says watchers are set over people, beginning a scene of deeds being observed that parallels the section’s Lord at the mirsad.
The next ayah identifies those watchers as noble recorders, specifying that observation becomes a preserved record.
The following ayah says they know what people do, completing the record-and-recompense parallel.
The following verse says what they had earned did not avail them; it adds the failure of their worldly works to the Thamud punishment example.
Salih reminds Thamud that they carve houses from mountains after building palaces on the plains; this repeats the specific stone-working image in 89:9.
Thamud are asked whether they carve houses from mountains proudly; it gives another explicit formulation of the rock-cutting that marks the section’s example.
The Thamud narrative says they hamstrung the she-camel; this supplies the specific transgression preceding the exemplary punishment of a people the section names.
The next ayah says punishment seized them, completing that act-to-recompense sequence for Thamud.
This account says Thamud were destroyed by the overwhelming blast, a concrete instance of the earlier exemplary punishments the section names.
The same account says Ad were destroyed by a furious wind, making another of the section’s named exempla an actual punishment scene.
Here Pharaoh and the overturned cities are named among those who came with wrongdoing, carrying the section’s Pharaoh example into a wider account of punished communities.
The next ayah says they disobeyed their Lord’s messenger and He seized them with an overwhelming seizure, specifying the recompense attached to 69:9’s named offenders.
This warning invokes a lightning strike like that of Ad and Thamud, showing those same peoples serving as prior punishment examples for another audience.
Ad’s denial is followed by the question of how the punishment and warnings were; this repeated warning formula makes one of the section’s examples explicitly didactic.
Thamud’s denial is likewise followed by the warning about punishment; it develops the section’s precedent-punishment image around its other named people.
Pharaoh’s people denied the signs and were seized; this is a direct narrative counterpart to the section’s naming Pharaoh among the exemplary punished.

In the story of two brothers, one says he will not extend his hand to kill the other if attacked. That is a specific refusal of reciprocal killing within the very family scene from which blood vengeance arises.
On the Day described here, a close friend does not ask after another; this reverses the section’s earthly image of a slain person’s kin pressing a claim, as final recompense exceeds their reach.
A person can see those close to him yet wish to ransom himself from the punishment; this develops the limit that a guardian cannot perform or avert the ultimate return.
The passage names wife and brother among the relatives who cannot serve as a substitute in that reckoning, a direct family boundary on the section’s human-wali image.
It expands the unavailable substitute to the clan that sheltered a person, sharpening the difference between human kinship and divine recompense.
The person would offer everyone on earth to be saved; no human substitute can meet the punishment described in the section’s final turn.
